items.title: GLM-5.3 (Fully Tested): I GOT EARLY ACCESS & IT'S #1 ON MY BENCH!
items.summary:
GLM Coding Plan (affiliate link - not sponsored): https://z.ai/subscribe?ic=NWKPDIY9WD

In this video, I'll be testing the new GLM-5.3 model from Z AI, which brings major improvements over GLM-5.2, especially in coding, security analysis, frontend generation, and complex benchmark tasks.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 GLM-5.3 is a major upgrade over GLM-5.2 while keeping the same parameter count and architecture.
🔐 The model is specialized in security analysis, code auditing, vulnerability discovery, and defensive AI use cases.
🛡️ Z AI is launching the Open-Source Shield initiative to make defensive capabilities more accessible while restricting high-risk misuse.
💻 GLM-5.3 shows major improvements in coding, frontend design, backend logic, simulations, and complex app generation.
📊 On KingBench 3, GLM-5.3 scores 73 out of 80, reaching 91.25 percent and taking the number 1 spot.
🏆 It beats Fable 5, Qwen 3.8 Max, Opus 4.8, Opus 5, and Kimi K3 on this benchmark.
⚡ GLM-5.3 improves from GLM-5.2’s 7
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] Hi, welcome to another video. So, the people at ZAI were kind enough to give me early access again, this time to GLM 5.3, which should be rolling out by the time you're watching this video. Now, I'll be honest with you, they haven't given me a ton of information about this one. What I know is that it is the same parameter count as before, same architecture and everything. It is basically GLM 5.2, too but post-trained further and just overall improved. But there is one interesting angle that they did share with me and it is a bit different from the usual benchmark talk. GLM 5.3 is specialized in security analysis. So it has specific strengths in code auditing, vulnerability discovery and security analysis. And this is not just a marketing line either. They told me that working with actual security teams, GLM 5.3 helped identify risks across developer tools, messaging apps, internet infrastructure, office systems, robotics. So they have been using this thing in the real world to find actual security issues which is pretty interesting. Now obviously a model that is good at that is a bit of a double-edged sword and ZAI knows that which is why they are launching something called the open- source shield initiative alongside it. The idea is that the defensive capabilities become more accessible to everyone while the high-risk misuse side is restricted through layered safeguards and trusted access so defenders get the good stuff openly and the dangerous stuff is gated. I think that's a pretty reasonable way to ship a model like this, especially as an open model. And the cool thing is that this security specialization seems to have made the model better at coding in general because if you think about it, a model that can audit code and reason about how things break is also a model that understands code deeply. And you can see that in my benchmark. So let's actually go through my own bench. I ran GLM 5.3 through Kingbench 3, which is the same set of questions that I have tested Fable 5, Opus 4.8, 8 Opus 5, Kimmy K3, Kuwen 3.8 Max, and basically everything else on so we can compare it directly. The first question is the elevator simulation where the user can spawn some people on different levels. Each person has a random floor that they want to go to and there are three elevators that can only take one person each. I like this one because there are a lot of caveats in it that models usually get wrong. GLM5.3 does really well here. The simulation logic is correct. One person gets on, the other one waits and gets picked up by the next elevator. The tool tips work and the animations are pretty smooth. It also doesn't look very AI generated, which I always appreciate. I have given it an eight here for reference. Fable got a nine on this one, so it is right up there. Next up, we've got the 3JS 3D model of a contact lens case with pronounced L and R caps that you can click to open. Now, this is the one where GLM 5.2 completely fell apart. It got a three last time. GLM 5.3 gets an eight. The case actually looks like a contact lens case. The L and R letters are big and clear. The caps unscrew and flip open when you click them. And there are even lenses inside. This is a massive jump on the exact same prompt in about 2 months. Then we have the 3JS folding table where there's a slider that folds and unfolds the table in 3D. GLM 5.3 gets a 10 here. It is seamless. The animation is smooth. The table looks like an actual table with proper legs and cross bracing. And the slider does exactly what it should. Fable got a nine on this one. So, it is literally beating Fable here. Then I asked it to make me an SVG of a panda eating a burger. And this is another 10. The panda is really cute. The burger is accurate. It has the little blush cheeks, the bamboo in the background, and even crumbs flying around the burger. This is one of the best panda generations that I have seen on this bench, period. Then we have the bow and arrow simulator game with four targets and a timebased leaderboard. Another 10. The game works well. The moving targets make it harder to play, which is what I actually want. The leaderboard persists, and it even verified its own game logic before telling me it was done. Fable got an aid on this one. So again, it is beating Fable. Then we have the mathematical question, which is a pretty hard permutation counting problem. The answer should be 2460. And GLM 5.3 nails it. That's a 10. Then there's one of the most complex prompts where I ask the model to generate a data set of pandacts, fine-tune a Gemma 2B model on it all on its own, fully locally, and then give me a web UI that generates a panda fact on every refresh. GLM 5.3 does the whole thing end to end. It generates the data set, runs the fine-tune, spins up the UI, and just hands me the local host URL. I didn't have to do anything. That's a 10. And finally, the hardest question on this bench, the working 3D wristwatch with smooth hands based on the current time, a date and day option, and two time zones. This is the question that destroys every model. Fable got a four, Opus 5 got a three. Most models get between zero and three. GLM 5.3 gets a seven, which is tied for the best score that I have ever given on this question. It built a proper dual time GMT watch. The hands actually track real time. The seconds sweep smoothly, the day-to-day windows work, and there's a second time zone on the bezel. It is not perfect, but it is genuinely the closest any model has come to what I actually asked for. So, this is the final chart, and GLM 5.3 scores 73 out of 80, which is 91.25%. That puts it at number one on Kingbench 3. Above Fable 5 at 82.5, above Quinn 3.8, max at 8125, above Opus 4.8 at 80, above Opus 5 and Kimmy K3 at 77.5. And just to put this in perspective, GLM 5.2 scored 75% on this same bench about 2 months ago. So we went from 75 to 91.25 in 2 months on the same parameter count. That is actually crazy. Now let me give you my honest thoughts. The model is just so good. I think that it beats Fable for me for sure. Fable is still good in extremely complex tasks and I would still reach for it when I have some really long horizon, really weird problem. But for everything else, we are now at 90 plus% of Fable openly for sure. And on my bench, it is literally above it. The model is also great at front end and back end alike. Usually, open models are decent at backend logic and then produce frontends that look like they came from 2023. This one does clean, dense, good-looking UI and solid backend work in the same task. The wristwatch and the fine-tuning question show both sides of that. And on top of all that, you get the security angle. If you have a codebase, you can just point this thing at it and ask it to audit for vulnerabilities. And that is an area where it is specifically trained to be strong. I think a lot of people are going to use it just for that. The pace here is what gets me. 2 months between releases, same parameters, and this kind of jump. If ZAI keeps this rate up, I genuinely don't know what the Frontier Labs are going to do about it. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this [music] video, consider donating through the super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join [music] button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. [music] >> [music]

items.title: Deepeek V4 Pro 0813 (Fully Tested): Okay, this is ACTUALLY CRAZY!
items.summary:
In this video, I'll be telling you about DeepSeek V4 Pro, the new model that quietly launched on the DeepSeek API, and why it might be one of the best price-to-performance AI models available right now.

--

🚀 DeepSeek V4 Pro is now officially available through the DeepSeek API.
📊 The model reportedly has 1.6 trillion parameters, 49 billion active parameters, and a 1 million token context window.

🎨 The model performs especially well in frontend, 3D, planning, reasoning, and long-horizon agentic tasks.

items.transcript: [music] >> Hi. Welcome to another video. So, DeepSeek V4 Pro is now officially available on their API. And in typical DeepSeek fashion, they just silently dropped it. There's no big launch event, no fancy live stream, and honestly, not even a ton of details about the model itself. They haven't shared much officially, but there is a benchmark table being shared around the internet with the model's official numbers. And the community has been digging up the rest. From what's circulating, this is reportedly a 1.6 trillion parameter model with 49 billion active parameters and a 1 million token context window. Take the exact specs with a grain of salt since DeepSeek themselves haven't been very loud about it. But that's what's floating around. The version that's live now is V4 Pro 0813, which is the proper release of the V4 Pro preview that we saw back in April. And the jump from that preview is honestly massive. On Terminal Bench 2.1, the preview was sitting at 72.1, and this new release scores 87.9. That's basically a 15.8 point jump on the same benchmark, and it puts it right next to Fable 5 at 88 and Kimiko 3 at 88.3. So, it's basically neck and neck with the absolute frontier models on terminal work. Now, let's look at that official benchmark table that's going around because it's actually quite interesting. On Cyber Gym, it scores 83.3, which is the best score on the whole table, just barely edging out Fable 5. On Automation Bench, it gets 31.8, which is also the best on the table, ahead of Kimiko 3 and Fable 5. On HLE, it gets 42.7 without tools and 60 with tools, which is behind Fable 5's 53.3 and 63, but still very respectable. Then on things like Deep Sway, Two Athlon, and the DS Bench evaluations, it's a few points behind Fable 5 and Opus 4.8, but it's playing in the same league. On NL2 Repo, Opus 4.8 still leads by a decent margin. So, the overall story from the official numbers is that this model is within a few points of the frontier on most agentic benchmarks. And it actually takes the top spot on a couple of them. But here's the thing that makes all of this crazy. The pricing. This model costs about 43 cents per million input tokens and 87 cents per million output tokens. Fable 5 is $10 and $50. That's why everyone, including the client team, is calling this the best price-to-performance model on the market right now because you're getting roughly Fable 5 level benchmark performance at around 57 times cheaper cost. And that's just wild. But you know how it goes on this channel. We don't just take the official numbers. I ran it through my own benchmark. So, let's get right into it. As always, I ran it through my King bench questions. These include some front-end and animation tasks, some 3JS tasks, an SVG test, a math problem, a long horizon agentic task, and one really hard 3D task at the end. Each question is scored out of 10, and at the end we'll look at the final chart to see where it lands in against the others. The first question is the elevator simulation. The model has to build a simulation where you can spawn people on different levels. There are three elevators. Each elevator can only take one person, and anyone left behind should catch the next elevator that comes. Let's send it and see. Okay, this gets a six out of 10. The core simulation is there, and it looks decent, but the elevator logic isn't fully correct in all cases. For context, the Opus models are sitting at 10 here, and Fable 5 and Kimiko 3 are at 9. But it's still a point better than V4 Flash, which got a five. So, it's a decent start, but not amazing. The second question is the 3JS contact lens case. It should be a 3D model of a contact lens case with pronounced L and R caps, and you should be able to click on the caps to open them up. This is a test where almost every model struggles. Let's send it and check. And this is an eight out of 10. The case looks right, the caps are labeled properly, and the click-to-open interaction works. That ties it with QN 3.8 Max Opus 5 and its own sibling V4 flash. The third question is the 3JS folding table. There's a slider and as you drag it to the right, the table should unfold and to the left it should fold back. It needs to be seamlessly animated and properly 3D. Let's send it. And this is a nine out of 10. The folding motion is smooth, the animation is seamless and the whole thing just [clears throat] works. That ties it with Fable 5, Kimik 3, GLM 5.2 and Sonnet 5 for the best score on this question. So, this is quite great to see. The fourth question is the SVG of a panda eating a burger. Like let's send it and see. And this one is a bit weak. It gets a five out of 10. The panda is recognizable, but the proportions are a bit off and the burger interaction isn't really convincing. Interestingly, Muse Spark 1.2 got a perfect 10 on this one and models like Kimik 3, GLM 5.2 and QN 3.8 Max are at eight. So, SVG generation is clearly not this model's strong suit. The fifth question is the bow and arrow simulator game. Four targets and hitting all the targets in the lowest time should put the player on the leaderboard. Let's send it and check. Okay, this gets a six out of 10. The shooting mechanic works and the targets are there. But the overall game feel and the leaderboard implementation aren't fully polished. The best models like Grok 4.5, QN 3.8 Max and the Opus models are at 10 here. So, this is just okay. The sixth question is the hard math problem about counting permutations of ordered pairs. And the answer should be 2,460. A lot of models completely fail this one. Let's send it and see. And it gets it exactly right. 2,460. Full 10 out of 10. That puts it in the same club as Fable 5, Opus 4.8, Kimik 3 and QN 3.8 Max. So, the reasoning side is clearly strong. The seventh question is the big long horizon one. Generate a data set of facts about pandas, finetune a Gemma 2B model on that data set and then build a local web UI that generates a a panda fact on every refresh, all of it autonomously, from scratch, fully local. Let's send it and see. And it's a full 10 out of 10. It generated the data set, ran the finetune, and served the whole thing through a local web UI without me having to intervene at any point. Most of the recent frontier models get a 10 here. And V4 Pro joins them without any drama. So, the agentic side is legit. The eighth and final question is the 3D wristwatch. A full working wristwatch in 3D that shows the actual current time with smooth second, minute, and hour hands, a date and day option, and two time zones. This is the hardest question on the bench, and no model had ever done well on it until recently. Let's send it. And believe it or not, this gets a seven out of 10. That is the best score any model has ever gotten on this question. For context, Fable 5 held the best score for a long time with just a four. Then V4 Flash and Muse Spark 1.2 pushed it to six. And now V4 Pro takes the crown with a seven. The watch actually comes together as a proper 3D wristwatch. The hands track real time smoothly, and the dual time zone option works. It's still not perfect, but this is genuinely impressive. So, this is the final chart, and DeepSeek V4 Pro ends up with 61 out of 80, which is 76.25%. That puts it in a tie with Muse Spark 1.2, just above GLM 5.2 at 75%, and its own sibling V4 Flash at 72.5%, and just below Kimmy K3 and Opus 5, which are at 77.5%, Fable 5 is still at the top with 82.5%, followed by Quinn 3.8 Max and Opus 4.8. And just to put the generational jump in perspective, the V4 Pro preview scored 24.8% on my bench. So, going from 24.8 to 76.25 is a remarkable step up from the previous versions. At this price point, sitting this close to models that cost 10 to 50 times more is honestly crazy. Now, let me also tell you about my actual experience using it outside the benchmark. Because the chart doesn't tell the full story here. First, the model still struggles with overthinking on simple problems. If you give it something trivial, it will sometimes sit there and reason about it way longer than it needs to, and that reasoning doesn't always help. In fact, this is where it gets interesting because in real life work, it's still sometimes worse than V4 Flash. Flash generally doesn't overthink that much, and even when it does overthink, it doesn't make mistakes because of it. The overthinking in Flash never really backfires. Here, it does. V4 Pro will sometimes think itself into a worse answer on a problem that Flash would have just solved directly. So, if you're doing simple day-to-day tasks, Flash might actually give you a better experience, which is a bit weird considering Pro is the bigger model. Second, the model is very overeager. It tries to fix simple stuff with complex methods. If there's a one-line fix, it might restructure half the file instead, add abstractions nobody asked for, and generally do way more than the task requires. And that makes it a not very good experience in some places because you end up reviewing a bunch of changes you never wanted. But, it's not all negative. The model is still remarkable in front-end work. The stuff it generates visually is genuinely on par with the frontier models. And you saw that with the folding table and the wristwatch scores. It's also really good in planning. When you give it a bigger task, the way it breaks things down and sequences the work is genuinely impressive. And one more thing that I really like. It's good at making sure that if the prompt is unclear, it asks for follow-ups instead of just running off and assuming things. A lot of models just guess and burn tokens going in the wrong direction. This one actually stops and asks, which saves you a lot of back and forth. So, what's the verdict? If you ask me, this is a really strong release. And at this price, it's honestly a no-brainer to at least try. It's a markable step up from the previous Deepcool versions. The official benchmarks mostly hold up and on my bench it lands right in the frontier neighborhood at a fraction of the cost. It's not a fable 5 killer and the overthinking and over eagerness mean that for simple everyday tasks V4 flash might still serve you better but for front end planning and bigger agentic work this is one of the best value models on the market right now. The best price to performance claim is not just marketing this time. Overall it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like [music] this video consider donating through the super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, [music] give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.
